title: PAUL SERVED GOD WITH TEARS—AND THAT CHANGES WHAT FAITHFULNESS LOOKS LIKE
paragraphs: PAUL SERVED GOD WITH TEARS—AND THAT CHANGES WHAT FAITHFULNESS LOOKS LIKE

We were taught to recognize faith by strength. Paul showed the Ephesian elders something far more uncomfortable: sometimes the clearest evidence that you have not abandoned God is the tears on your face while you keep serving Him.
There are tears nobody at church ever sees.
You wipe them away before walking through the door.
You straighten your clothes. Fix your face. Open your Bible. Smile when someone asks how you are doing.
“I'm good.”
But you are not good.
Something inside you is exhausted.
You have prayed about the same thing so many times that you are beginning to feel embarrassed mentioning it to God again.
You have worshiped while wondering why heaven seems silent.
You have encouraged people while privately needing someone to encourage you.
You have served while hurting.
Given while empty.
Loved while disappointed.
Forgiven while still bleeding from what happened.
And somewhere along the way, perhaps you quietly started believing something terrifying:
Maybe if my faith were stronger, I wouldn't hurt this much.
Then Paul stands on a shoreline near Miletus and destroys that illusion.
He is saying goodbye to men he loves.

Luke tells us that Paul summoned the elders of the church in Ephesus. These were not strangers listening to a polished testimony. These men had watched his life. They knew what happened when the meetings ended. They knew what his ministry actually cost.
So Paul could not impress them with religious performance.
Instead, he reminded them of something they had already witnessed.
In the Greek text of Acts 20:19, Paul describes himself this way:
δουλεύων τῷ Κυρίῳ μετὰ πάσης ταπεινοφροσύνης καὶ δακρύων
douleuōn tō Kyriō meta pasēs tapeinophrosynēs kai dakryōn
Literally, the thought is:
“Serving the Lord with all humility and with tears.”
With tears.
Do not rush past those two words.
The apostle Paul—the missionary, preacher, church planter, theologian, prisoner, defender of the Gospel—did not tell these elders, “You remember how powerful I looked.”
He reminded them that they had seen him cry.
And the Greek makes something especially beautiful clear.
The word δουλεύων (douleuōn) comes from douleuō, carrying the idea of serving as a servant. Paul understood himself as belonging to the Lord.
But notice what stands beside his service.
δακρύων.
dakryōn.
Tears.
His tears were not evidence that he had stopped serving.
They accompanied his service.
That distinction may be exactly what somebody reading this needs tonight.
You can be hurting and faithful at the same time.
You can be grieving and obedient at the same time.
You can have questions and still follow Jesus.
You can cry during the prayer and still mean every word of it.
You can walk into tomorrow without understanding what God is doing and still whisper, “Jesus, I belong to You.”
Faithfulness is not emotional numbness.
Paul's tears prove it.

And these were not theatrical tears manufactured to make a sermon more moving. Acts places them inside the pressure of real ministry. Paul speaks about trials and opposition. He reminds the elders that he withheld nothing profitable from them, teaching publicly and from house to house. Then he summarizes the heartbeat of his message: repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.
That matters.
Because biblical Christianity is not merely learning how to survive difficult emotions.
The center is Jesus.
The call is repentance.
The promise is grace.
Paul did not spend three years telling people simply to believe in themselves, discover their potential, protect their peace, or manifest a better future.
He pointed sinners toward God.
He pointed them toward Christ.

Repentance means we cannot merely blame everything outside ourselves. Somewhere beneath our wounds are sins we must confess, idols we must surrender, bitterness we must release, pride we must crucify, secret compromises we must drag into the light.
And faith means we do not save ourselves after discovering what is wrong with us.
We run to Jesus.
That is the Gospel.
Not “repair yourself until God accepts you.”
Christ came for sinners.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose from the grave.
Forgiveness is not purchased by our tears.
Grace is not God's reward for people who suffer beautifully.
Our hope rests in Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is why Paul's tears are so powerful.
They belonged to a man who knew grace.
Before Paul became the man crying over churches, he was the man persecuting the church.
Think about that.
There had been another version of Paul.
A feared version.
A violent version.
A man whose religious zeal had become persecution.
Acts introduces Saul approving the killing of Stephen, and then describes him ravaging the church and dragging believers away.
If you had frozen Paul's story there, you might have thought you knew how it ended.
Enemy.
Persecutor.
Destroyer.
Scandal.
But Jesus had not finished writing.
On the road to Damascus, Saul encountered the risen Christ.
The persecutor became a preacher.
The man once associated with suffering inflicted upon Christians eventually became a man willing to suffer for Christ.
The hands connected with persecution would become hands that worked to support ministry.
The mouth that once opposed Jesus would proclaim Him.
The eyes once burning with hostility would fill with tears over Christ's people.
That is not self-improvement.
That is grace.
That is what Jesus does.
He does not merely polish reputations.
He resurrects lives.
And maybe you need that because there is a chapter of your own story you desperately wish could be torn out.
Something you did.
Something you became.
Someone you hurt.
Years you wasted.
A secret nobody knows.
A season when you walked away from God.
A marriage damaged by your choices.
A child you failed.
An addiction you kept feeding.
A compromise you kept defending.
A version of yourself that still appears in your memories at two in the morning and whispers:
“After everything you've done, who do you think you are to come back to God?”
Look again at Paul.
The Gospel does not pretend the scandal never happened.
The Gospel declares that the scandal does not have to write the final sentence.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by pretending sin does not matter.
Not by erasing repentance.
Jesus transforms sinners through grace.
The cross proves simultaneously how serious our sin is and how extraordinary God's mercy is.
Paul knew this personally.
So when this man speaks about grace, he is not discussing an abstract doctrine.
He is describing the reason he is standing there at all.
Then the farewell becomes even heavier.
Paul tells the elders that he is going toward Jerusalem without knowing exactly what will happen there. What he does know is sobering: imprisonment and afflictions await him.
Imagine knowing suffering is ahead...
and walking forward anyway.
Most of us want God to show us the safe road.
Paul was willing to obey on the dangerous one.
Acts 20:24 reveals why. His overriding concern was finishing the course and ministry he had received from the Lord Jesus: bearing witness to the Gospel of God's grace.
There it is again.
Grace.
The former persecutor is now willing to suffer so other people can hear about the grace that rescued him.
Maybe this is where Paul's story stops being comfortable.
Because many of us are willing to follow Jesus as long as following Jesus does not cost too much.
We want Christianity with manageable inconvenience.
We want a cross that matches the furniture.
We want resurrection without dying to ourselves.
We want Jesus as Savior while quietly negotiating whether He may truly be Lord.
But Paul says, in effect:
My life is not the treasure I am protecting.
Christ gave me a mission.
I intend to finish it.
And still...
he cried.
Do you see the strange beauty?
Courage and tears occupied the same body.
Conviction and tenderness lived in the same man.
Paul did not become courageous by becoming emotionally cold.
He became courageous because Christ mattered more than his comfort.
Later in the same farewell, Paul returns to the tears.
He tells the elders to remember that for three years he had warned them night and day “with tears.”
Three years.
Night and day.
With tears.
These were shepherd's tears.
Tears for people.
Tears because truth matters.
Tears because souls matter.
Tears because deception destroys.
Tears because Paul understood that ministry is not content production. People are not numbers. Congregations are not audiences. The Gospel is not a brand.
These were human beings for whom Christ died.
That should confront every Christian who has learned how to discuss theology without loving people.
You can win an argument and lose tenderness.
You can know doctrine and become proud.
You can defend truth while secretly enjoying humiliating the person who is wrong.
Paul would not recognize that as spiritual maturity.
His doctrine had tears in it.
His warnings had tears in them.
His leadership had tears in it.
His courage had tears in it.
His ministry had tears in it.
And then something happens at the end of Acts 20 that is almost unbearably human.
Paul finishes speaking.
He kneels.
They pray.
And everybody begins crying.
These grown men embrace Paul and kiss him.
They know this is goodbye.
Luke tells us what hurt them most: Paul had said they would not see his face again.
Notice that Scripture does not sanitize the scene.
Nobody says, “Stop crying. Paul is going to heaven someday.”
Nobody rebukes them for grief.
Nobody tells them that strong Christians should smile because God has a plan.
They weep.
Because love makes goodbye hurt.
Christian hope does not require us to pretend loss is painless.
Jesus Himself wept at Lazarus's tomb.
The Son of God knew resurrection was coming, and still He wept.
That means tears and faith are not enemies.
Sometimes tears are what love looks like when words can no longer carry the weight.
So perhaps you have misunderstood your tears.
Maybe you thought crying meant God was disappointed with you.
Maybe somebody taught you that mature believers never collapse.
Maybe you have been hiding because everyone thinks you are the strong one.
Pastors cry.
Mothers cry.
Fathers cry.
Missionaries cry.
Leaders cry.
People who know Scripture cry.
People filled with faith cry.
People walking in obedience cry.
Paul served the Lord...
with tears.
But there is another side of this message that we cannot avoid.
Not every tear proves faithfulness.
We can cry over consequences without repenting of sin.
We can feel emotional during worship and refuse to surrender.
We can be moved by Jesus without actually following Jesus.
Paul's message was not merely tears.
It was repentance toward God and faith in the Lord Jesus.
So this is where the question becomes personal.
What are your tears producing?
Are they pushing you toward Jesus...
or merely deeper into yourself?
Are you asking God only to remove the pain...
or are you willing to let Him expose what needs to change?
Are you asking Jesus to comfort you while refusing to surrender the thing He has already told you to release?
Because grace comforts us, yes.
But grace also transforms us.
Jesus did not die merely to make us feel better while we remain enslaved to the same sin.
He came to save.
To forgive.
To cleanse.
To reconcile.
To make us new.
Maybe you have been pretending for too long.
Tonight, you do not need another performance.
You need Jesus.
Tell Him the truth.
Tell Him you are tired.
Tell Him where you sinned.
Tell Him what you are afraid of.
Tell Him what you have been hiding.
Tell Him about the anger.
The pornography.
The pride.
The jealousy.
The bitterness.
The affair.
The secret messages.
The addiction.
The unbelief.
The resentment toward God.
The shame.
Bring it into the light.
Repentance is not running away from God because you have been exposed.
It is turning toward Him because Christ opened the way home.
You may come with tears.
Just come.
There is something else Paul tells those elders before he leaves.
He commends them to God and to “the word of His grace.”
Paul knows he cannot stay.
He cannot protect them forever.
He cannot answer every future question.
He cannot prevent every wolf from coming.
So eventually Paul must release the people he loves into hands stronger than his own.
God's hands.
Perhaps you need to do that too.
There is someone you cannot fix.
A child you cannot control.
A spouse you cannot change.
A loved one you cannot force to believe.
A situation you cannot hold together no matter how tightly your fingers are wrapped around it.
You have prayed.
You have warned.
You have cried.
You have tried.
There comes a moment when faith sounds like:
“Jesus, I cannot carry this person as if I were their savior. You are the Savior. I entrust them to You.”
That surrender may come with tears.
Let it.
Paul's did.
And perhaps this is the sentence you should remember tomorrow when the pain returns:
You do not have to stop crying before you can keep following Jesus.
Cry...
and pray.
Cry...
and obey.
Cry...
and forgive.
Cry...
and repent.
Cry...
and open the Bible again.
Cry...
and show up.
Cry...
and worship.
Cry...
and keep your eyes on Christ.
Because sometimes faith does not look like walking through the fire without tears.
Sometimes faith looks like walking through the fire while the tears are still falling, because you have decided Jesus is worthy even here.
Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer needed tonight.
Do not keep this message trapped on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Christ alone saves, and grace cannot be bought.

But if this ministry is helping people encounter Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and Jesus Christ, supporting and sharing that work can be one practical way of helping biblical encouragement reach someone else. If you want your support to glorify God, let it come from gratitude rather than guilt—from a desire to see Christ proclaimed rather than from any thought that you can purchase His approval.
Look at Jesus.
Paul's tears matter because Paul's Lord matters.
The Savior Paul proclaimed is the Savior who received sinners.
The Savior who touched lepers.
The Savior who welcomed the broken.
The Savior who called people to repentance.
The Savior who wept.
The Savior who carried the cross.
The Savior whose blood was shed for sinners.
The Savior who was buried.
The Savior who rose.
The Savior who confronted a persecutor named Saul and turned his entire story around.
And He is still saving sinners.
Still restoring wanderers.
Still breaking chains.
Still forgiving the repentant.
Still rebuilding what sin shattered.
Still receiving people who finally stop pretending.
So if your face is wet with tears while you read these final words, perhaps you do not need to wipe them away yet.
Talk to Jesus.
The tears are not too much for Him.
The past is not too scandalous for His grace.
The wound is not hidden from His eyes.
The sin is not something you need to disguise.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come believing.
Come exhausted if necessary.
But come to Christ.
And tomorrow, when you wake up and discover that everything has not magically become easy, remember an apostle standing before beloved elders saying that he served the Lord with humility...
and tears.
Then remember something even greater.
Paul's story did not begin with Paul's faithfulness.
It began with Christ's mercy.
And yours does too.
And before you leave, comment one sentence—not for an algorithm, but as an honest confession before a community that also knows what it means to struggle:
“Jesus, I will serve You even through my tears.”
Because one day you may discover that the tears you thought proved you were falling apart were falling from the face of someone Christ was teaching to depend completely on Him.
Your tears do not get the final sentence. Jesus does.
